You can buy a very basic 3D printer for 300 quid. An industry grade one for 5000. Plastic filament? MAYBE 10 bucks for your pyramid. Make a pyramid in free CAD (the video mentions financial cost only.) Section it. Print Sections. You have a sectioned pyramid for less than 400 quid. Better yet? Silicon for the moulds, resin/plastic for pouring. Want to make it smooth? Sandpaper, primer. MAYBE an extra 100 quid. Make silicon moulds of pyramid sections. 500 quid. Smooth, sectioned pyramids galore. To break even on your first 1000, you charge 50c each. It's enormously disingenuous to quote 17,000 and name aluminium moulds which are industrial standard for mass manufacturing. I also seriously question the premise that people are more worried about losing tasks than jobs. In the literal sense, my stability doesn’t depend on my completion of tasks, it depends on a job, which is a series of tasks. AI can automate a whole number of tasks without sufficiently automating enough tasks to constitute the entire job, ergo, I am worried about losing my job, not the tasks it's comprised of. And finally, the atm and all arguments of the same ilk are an apples to oranges example. Technological innovations like the calculator replaced one task. A calculator can't produce anything new, it can't compute formulas without its user having the knowledge to input them. Computers have produced an unpredictably vast number of jobs. As they progress, they automate some jobs, and augment most. Crucially, the market adapts to losses by going into deeper systems that are harder to automate. AI is not comparable for that one explicit reason: yes, it will automate many of the jobs that are created in its wake, assuming those jobs are done on computers, and far far beyond the scope of any other innovation in history, but more importantly, its application is already so laterally broad and its capacity so deep that any new jobs created in its wake that it can't automate may require such a large jump in education and reskilling than many people either wont be able to afford the jump in terms of educational costs, will be too late to adapt to the steep curve, or simply won't be able to attain the depth of knowledge required. Comparisons with photoshop and excel fundamentally misunderstand the scope of an LLMs capability, and I think people need to understand that. It won't help anyone to say otherwise. The reason why that hasnt happened yet is a matter of competency and scalability, and by extension, financial cost and energy constraints. Open source models are already reducing cost substantially, which frees up development costs. As advances are made in terms of memory and compute, those advances will translate to more complex models and greater competency. The energy problem is the only serious obstacle, and the push for small modular reactors will eventually win ground in the name of economic growth, and the last obstacle vanishes. I have zero support for AI, and I truly hope the entire industry collapses, as a full disclosure. But this video is badly misinformed.
